question: What makes a chemical reaction exothermic?

passages.title: Exothermic reaction - Wikipedia
passages.text: Exothermic reaction In thermochemistry, an exothermic reaction is a "reaction for which the overall standard enthalpy change ΔH⚬ is negative."[1][2] Exothermic reactions usually release stored energy as heat. The term is often confused with exergonic reaction, which IUPAC defines as "... a reaction for which the overall standard Gibbs energy change ΔG⚬ is negative."[2] A strongly exothermic reaction will usually also be exergonic because ΔH⚬ makes a major contribution to ΔG⚬. Most of the spectacular chemical reactions that are demonstrated in classrooms are exothermic and exergonic. The opposite is an endothermic reaction, which usually takes up heat and is driven by an entropy increase in the system. Examples Examples are numerous: combustion, the thermite reaction, combining strong acids and bases, polymerizations. Easy Exothermic Examples to Observe Several everyday activities demonstrate the release of heat during chemical reactions or physical changes. Reusable Hand Warmers: Some reusable hand warmers contain a supersaturated solution of sodium acetate. Activating the metal disc inside the pouch starts crystallization, releasing heat. This is an exothermic physical process rather than a chemical reaction. Dissolving Calcium Chloride: Adding a small amount of pure calcium chloride to water causes the temperature to increase as the salt dissolves. This is an easy classroom demonstration using a thermometer. Wear eye protection and avoid direct contact with the chemical or solution. Burning a Candle: Combustion is an example of an exothermic chemical reaction. Lighting a candle provides the initial energy needed to begin the reaction between vaporized wax and oxygen. Once burning, the candle releases heat and light. Use appropriate fire safety precautions and adult supervision. These examples also illustrate an important distinction: A process can release heat without being a chemical reaction.

Examples of Exothermic Processes Not every exothermic process is a chemical reaction. Physical changes can also release heat without producing new chemical substances. Examples include: - Freezing: Liquid water releases heat as it changes into ice. - Condensation: Water vapor releases heat when it condenses into liquid droplets, such as those forming clouds and rain. - Deposition: Water vapor releases heat when it changes directly into ice crystals, as occurs during some types of snow formation. - Dissolving calcium chloride: Anhydrous calcium chloride releases heat when it dissolves in water. -

passages.text: Exothermic process In thermodynamics, an exothermic process (from Ancient Greek έξω (éxō) 'outward' and θερμικός (thermikós) 'thermal')[1] is a thermodynamic process or reaction that releases energy from the system to its surroundings,[2] usually in the form of heat, but also in a form of light (e.g. a spark, flame, or flash), electricity (e.g. a battery), or sound (e.g. explosion heard when burning hydrogen). The term exothermic was coined by 19th-century French chemist Marcellin Berthelot.[3] The opposite of an exothermic process is an endothermic process, one that absorbs energy, usually in the form of heat.[2] The concept is frequently applied in the physical sciences to chemical reactions where chemical bond energy is converted to thermal energy (heat). passages.title: What Makes a Chemical Reaction Exothermic? - Biology Insights
passages.text: An exothermic reaction is a chemical process characterized by the release of energy into the surrounding environment. This energy is most commonly experienced as heat, causing the temperature of the surroundings to increase noticeably. The term “exothermic” literally means “out of heat,” describing this outward flow of thermal energy. Highly exothermic reactions may also release energy as light, such as the flame seen when wood burns. This energy transfer powers many natural and industrial processes. The Role of Chemical Bonds The fundamental reason a chemical reaction releases heat lies in the energy dynamics of breaking and forming chemical bonds. All chemical reactions begin with the breaking of existing bonds in the reactant molecules, which requires a specific input of energy. This initial energy input is known as the activation energy. Breaking a bond is always a process that absorbs energy from the surroundings. Once the initial bonds are broken, the atoms rearrange themselves to form new, more stable chemical bonds, creating the product molecules. The formation of any chemical bond is a process that inherently releases energy. This is the principle behind reusable hand warmers and the “hot ice” demonstration. Nuclear reactions can also release large amounts of energy. For example, nuclear fission produces energy that can be converted into heat, but fission is a nuclear reaction rather than a chemical reaction. How to Tell If a Reaction Is Exothermic The most direct way to identify an exothermic reaction is to measure the temperature of its surroundings. When a reaction releases heat to its surroundings, their temperature generally increases. A thermometer or calorimeter provides a more reliable measurement than touching the reaction container. In chemical equations and thermodynamic calculations, an exothermic reaction has a negative enthalpy change (ΔH < 0). On an enthalpy diagram, the products appear at a lower energy level than the reactants. However, a reaction may release heat so slowly that no noticeable temperature increase occurs. Rusting is one example.

Endothermic and Exothermic Reactions Endothermic and exothermic reactions can be thought of as having energy as either a reactant of the reaction or a product. Endothermic reactions require energy, so energy is a reactant. Heat flows from the surroundings to the system (reaction mixture) and the enthalpy of the system increases (\(\Delta H\) is positive). As discussed in the previous section, heat is released (considered a product) in an exothermic reaction, and the enthalpy of the system decreases (\(\Delta H\) is negative). In the course of an endothermic process, the system gains heat from the surroundings and so the temperature of the surroundings decreases (gets cold). A chemical reaction is exothermic if heat is released by the system into the surroundings. Because the surroundings is gaining heat from the system, the temperature of the surroundings increases. passages.title: Exothermic Reactions – Definition and Examples
passages.text: Exothermic reactions are chemical reactions that release heat to their surroundings. These reactions often cause the surroundings to become warmer, although the temperature change may be too small or gradual to notice. Some exothermic reactions, such as combustion, produce enough heat to generate flames or cause explosions. During a chemical reaction, breaking bonds requires energy, while forming bonds releases energy. An exothermic reaction releases more energy through bond formation than it absorbs through bond breaking. As a result, the products have a lower enthalpy than the reactants. The enthalpy change (ΔH) of an exothermic reaction is negative: ΔH < 0 This means heat flows from the reacting system to its surroundings. However, some exothermic reactions require an initial input of energy, called activation energy, before they begin. This enthalpy change represents the amount of heat energy transferred between the chemical system and its surroundings during the process. The change in enthalpy is calculated by subtracting the total energy of the reactants from the total energy of the products. For a reaction to be classified as exothermic, the products must possess a lower heat content than the initial reactants. Subtracting a larger reactant energy value from a smaller product energy value results in a negative number for \(\Delta H\). This negative sign is the universal indicator of an exothermic reaction, signifying that heat has left the chemical system. For instance, the combustion of methane has an enthalpy change of approximately \(-890\) kilojoules per mole, indicating a substantial release of heat. Common Exothermic Processes Combustion is one of the most familiar examples of an exothermic process, which involves a substance reacting rapidly with oxygen to produce heat and light. These examples also illustrate an important distinction: A process can release heat without being a chemical reaction. Frequently Asked Questions Do All Exothermic Reactions Produce Heat? Yes. By definition, an exothermic reaction releases heat. Some reactions also produce light or sound, but heat release is the defining characteristic. The temperature increase may be too small to notice, particularly if the reaction occurs slowly. Why Do Some Exothermic Reactions Need Heat to Start? Exothermic reactions can require an initial input of energy to overcome an activation energy barrier. For example, a candle needs a flame to ignite its wax vapor, but the combustion reaction releases heat once it begins. The overall reaction releases more energy than is required to initiate it. Are All Exothermic Reactions Spontaneous? No. Whether a reaction is thermodynamically spontaneous depends on the Gibbs free energy change (ΔG), which includes the effects of both enthalpy and entropy. An exothermic reaction may be nonspontaneous under certain conditions. Additionally, a thermodynamically spontaneous reaction may proceed extremely slowly because of a large activation energy. Measurement The enthalpy of a chemical system is essentially its energy. The enthalpy change ΔH for a reaction is equal to the heat q transferred out of (or into) a closed system at constant pressure without in- or output of electrical energy. Heat production or absorption in a chemical reaction is measured using calorimetry, e.g. with a bomb calorimeter. One common laboratory instrument is the reaction calorimeter, where the heat flow from or into the reaction vessel is monitored. The heat release and corresponding energy change, ΔH, of a combustion reaction can be measured particularly accurately. The measured heat energy released in an exothermic reaction is converted to ΔH⚬ in Joule per mole (formerly cal/mol). Terms Related to Exothermic Reaction Exergonic Reaction: An exergonic reaction is a reaction with a negative Gibbs free energy change (ΔG < 0). Exergonic reactions are thermodynamically favorable under the specified conditions. Exothermic and exergonic reactions are not necessarily the same. Exothermic describes heat release, while exergonic describes a decrease in Gibbs free energy, which depends on both enthalpy and entropy. Endothermic Reaction: An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings. In an endothermic reaction, the enthalpy change is positive (ΔH > 0). Some release heat rapidly, while others proceed slowly enough that the temperature change is difficult to detect. Examples of exothermic chemical reactions include: - Combustion: Burning wood, natural gas, candle wax, or sugar releases heat and often light. - Neutralization: The reaction between a strong acid and a strong base, such as hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, releases heat. - Rusting: Iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form rust. The reaction releases heat, but the process is usually too slow to produce a noticeable temperature increase. - Cellular respiration: The overall oxidation of glucose releases energy. Cells capture some of this energy in ATP, while some is released as heat. - Hydration: Adding water to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate releases heat as the hydrated compound forms. - Formation of sodium chloride: Sodium reacts with chlorine to form sodium chloride (table salt), releasing considerable heat. - The thermite reaction: A highly exothermic reaction between a metal oxide and a more reactive metal, usually aluminum. - Potassium permanganate and glycerol: This strongly exothermic oxidation reaction can produce flames. -

In an exothermic reaction, the amount of energy released when the new bonds form is significantly greater than the energy that was initially absorbed to break the old bonds. For instance, the products often feature much stronger bonds than the reactants, which accounts for the large energy difference. This difference creates a net surplus of energy that cannot remain within the chemical system. The excess energy is expelled into the environment, typically as heat, making the reaction exothermic. Reactant molecules hold more stored chemical potential energy than the product molecules they transform into. This conversion of higher-energy reactants into lower-energy products drives the release of heat. Measuring Energy Change with Enthalpy Chemists use the concept of enthalpy, represented by the symbol \(H\), to quantify the heat content of a system at a constant pressure. The absolute enthalpy of a substance cannot be directly measured, so scientists focus on the change in enthalpy (\(\Delta H\)) between the start and end of a reaction.
